title: GC & Memory in Production
scopeHtml: Diagnosing real memory failures: leaks, OOM kinds, heap dumps, native/off-heap memory, humongous allocation, and long pauses, with numbers.

questions.promptHtml: "OutOfMemoryError" is not one error. List the kinds you have seen in production, what memory area each one points at, and the first thing you check for each.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates who say "increase -Xmx" for every OOM have never debugged one. The signal is whether you read the message text and map it to a memory region.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The text after "OutOfMemoryError:" tells me the region. "Java heap space" is heap: leak or undersized heap. "GC overhead limit exceeded" is heap thrashing. "Metaspace" is class metadata, usually a classloader leak or runaway class generation. "Direct buffer memory" is NIO/Netty off-heap hitting MaxDirectMemorySize. "unable to create native thread" is the OS refusing a thread: ulimit, PID cgroup limit, or native memory exhausted. And a container OOM-kill is not a Java exception at all: the kernel killed the process with exit code 137, and the heap may have been fine.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A JVM process is more than the heap:

Process RSS = Java heap
            + Metaspace (class metadata, native)
            + Code cache (JIT output)
            + Thread stacks (N threads x -Xss, default 1 MB on 64-bit Linux)
            + Direct/mapped buffers (NIO, Netty)
            + GC data structures (remembered sets, card tables, mark bitmaps)
            + JNI / native libs / glibc malloc arenas

Each region has its own limit and its own failure message:

Message Region Typical cause First check
Java heap space Heap Leak, or live set > Xmx Heap dump, post-GC heap trend
GC overhead limit exceeded Heap (Parallel GC) Live set ~ Xmx, GC thrashing Same as above
Metaspace Metaspace Classloader leak, dynamic proxies/codegen jcmd GC.class_stats / jcmd VM.metaspace, class count trend
Direct buffer memory Off-heap Netty/NIO buffer not released, many big buffers MaxDirectMemorySize, buffer pool MBeans
unable to create native thread OS threads Thread leak, ulimit -u, cgroup pids.max, low native memory Thread count, ulimit -u, pids.max
Requested array size exceeds VM limit Heap Array near Integer.MAX_VALUE Code allocating a huge array
(no message) exit 137 Container RSS > cgroup memory limit NMT, RSS vs heap, container memory metrics

Only the first six are java.lang.OutOfMemoryError thrown by the JVM; the last is the Linux OOM killer sending SIGKILL, so no stack trace, no heap dump (unless you triggered one earlier), and -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError does nothing.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
(flags to make OOMs diagnosable)

-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError
-XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps/        # a mounted volume, not the container FS
-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError     # die and let the orchestrator restart, rather than limp
-Xlog:gc*:file=/logs/gc.log:time,uptime:filecount=5,filesize=20m

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Raising -Xmx on a "Metaspace" or "native thread" OOM: it makes the native OOM more likely, because the heap takes memory from the same container budget.
  • Dumping to the container's ephemeral disk: a 6 GB dump fills it and the pod is evicted.
  • Leaving the process alive after an OOM: other threads may have died silently with inconsistent state. Prefer ExitOnOutOfMemoryError plus restart.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does an OOM in one thread kill the JVM? -> No, only that thread's task fails; the JVM continues, which is why half-dead services exist. Use ExitOnOutOfMemoryError or CrashOnOutOfMemoryError.
  2. Why no heap dump on container kill? -> SIGKILL cannot be handled; the JVM never gets to run any hook.
  3. Why can "Java heap space" occur with free heap? -> Contiguous space needed for a huge array or a G1 humongous allocation can't be found even though total free is large (see the humongous question).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "heap is full, increase Xmx". Senior: maps each message to a region, knows exit 137 is not an exception, sets dump and exit flags ahead of time, and budgets container memory as heap + non-heap.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams routinely discover during an incident that no heap dump exists because the path was unwritable or the kernel killed the process first.

questions.promptHtml: Java has garbage collection. How can a Java application still have a memory leak?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests the correct definition of reachability-based leaks, the foundation for every leak question after it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The GC frees objects that are unreachable from GC roots. A Java leak is an object that is still reachable but will never be used again. Something holds a reference, typically a static map, a cache without eviction, a listener never deregistered, a ThreadLocal on a pooled thread, or a classloader that cannot unload. GC cannot know your intent, so it keeps them forever and the live set grows until OOM or GC thrash.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
GC roots are thread stacks, static fields of loaded classes, JNI references, and some VM internals. Marking walks the object graph from roots; anything not marked is garbage. So "leak" means: an unwanted path from a root exists.

GC root (static field) --> HashMap --> Entry --> Session --> 2 MB of state
                           ^ nobody removes entries => path stays alive

Symptoms to distinguish from "just busy":

  • Healthy: heap sawtooths, and the low points (post-full-GC or post-mixed floor) are flat.
  • Leak: the floor rises monotonically across hours/days; GC frequency and pause grow; eventually OOM or "GC overhead".

Common sources: static collections, unbounded caches (use Caffeine with maximumSize/expireAfter), listeners/callbacks (observer never removed), inner classes capturing this, ThreadLocals, ClassLoader retention, interned or substring-retained data, unclosed resources (streams, JDBC statements holding native memory), and metrics registries with unbounded tag cardinality (a new Micrometer time series per user id).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Broken {
    private static final Map<String, byte[]> CACHE = new HashMap<>();
    static byte[] load(String key) {
        return CACHE.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new byte[1_000_000]); // never evicted
    }
}
// Fix: bounded cache
// Cache<String, byte[]> cache = Caffeine.newBuilder().maximumSize(500).expireAfterAccess(Duration.ofMinutes(10)).build();

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling System.gc() hoping to fix it: reachable objects are never freed.
  • Confusing a high heap with a leak: with a large Xmx the collector simply delays collections; look at the post-GC floor, not peak.
  • Forgetting that unbounded metric labels are a leak.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you prove it's a leak, not load? -> Post-GC occupancy floor trend over hours plus two heap dumps diffed in MAT.
  2. Do WeakReferences fix leaks? -> They allow collection when no strong refs exist; WeakHashMap with a value that strongly refs its key still leaks.
  3. Can a leak exist off-heap? -> Yes: direct buffers, JNI, Unsafe; GC can't see or bound them well. See the NMT question.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE gives "static collections". Senior defines leak as unintended reachability, names the post-GC floor as the signal, and lists non-obvious sources (metric cardinality, classloader, ThreadLocal).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A service whose per-request tracing tags created a new time series each call slowly consumed 6 GB over a week and "looked like" a GC problem.

questions.promptHtml: What are allocation rate and live set, and how does each affect GC pause time and frequency?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: These two numbers drive almost every GC tuning decision. A senior can predict GC behavior from them.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Allocation rate is how many MB/s the application creates; it determines how often young collections happen. Live set is how much data survives collections; it determines how long each collection takes, since copying/marking cost scales with live data, not garbage. High allocation with a small live set gives frequent, cheap young GCs. A large or growing live set gives longer pauses and eventually full GCs.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Young GC frequency ~ young size / allocation rate. Example: 2 GB eden, 400 MB/s allocation => a young GC every 5 s. Pause time ~ work proportional to survivors copied plus roots and remembered sets scanned, not eden size. Dead objects cost nothing in a copying collector.

Allocation rate  -> HOW OFTEN   (young GC every eden/rate seconds)
Live set/survivors -> HOW LONG  (copy cost; old-gen marking cost)
Promotion rate   -> how fast old gen fills -> mixed/full GC frequency

Estimating from a GC log: allocation rate = (heap-before-GC(n) - heap-after-GC(n-1)) / time between GCs. Live set ~ heap after a full/mixed-cycle completion.

Levers: reduce allocation (reuse buffers, avoid boxing, avoid copies in JSON/serialization) lowers frequency; bigger young gen reduces frequency but not per-GC cost (and may raise it if survivors grow); reducing live set (smaller caches, off-heap, better data structures) lowers pause time and old-gen pressure.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
(quick measurement)

jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000      # watch E (eden) fill speed and YGC/FGC counters
jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s settings=profile filename=/tmp/a.jfr  # allocation profiling

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing a bigger heap means longer pauses always: for young GC, pause tracks survivors, so a bigger young gen can keep pauses equal while cutting frequency.
  • Tuning flags before measuring allocation rate.
  • Forgetting premature promotion: survivors overflow, short-lived objects reach old gen, and old-gen GC rises.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Allocation rate is 1.2 GB/s with 600 MB eden, what do you see? -> A young GC about every 0.5 s; premature promotion likely; first reduce allocation or enlarge young.
  2. Why can a young GC be slow with little garbage? -> Large survivors, big remembered sets, or many thread roots.
  3. What does G1 do with the pause target? -> It sizes young regions to meet MaxGCPauseMillis (default 200 ms) using its prediction model, trading frequency for pause length.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "more memory fixes GC". Senior computes GC interval from the allocation rate, ties pause length to live set/survivors, and attacks allocation at its source with a profiler.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A JSON-heavy service cut young GC frequency 3x by streaming rather than building intermediate strings, with zero flag changes.

questions.promptHtml: You have a 4 GB heap dump from a leaking service. Walk me through analyzing it in Eclipse MAT. What are shallow heap, retained heap, and the dominator tree, and why do they matter?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who have actually opened a dump from those who only know the word "jmap".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Shallow heap is the object's own size. Retained heap is memory that would be freed if that object were collected: everything only reachable through it. The dominator tree arranges objects by who keeps whom alive, sorted by retained size, so the biggest retainers float to the top. I run the Leak Suspects report, then open the dominator tree, then use "Path to GC Roots (exclude weak/soft refs)" on a suspicious object to see which static field or thread holds it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
MAT parses the hprof, builds an index, and computes dominators. Object A dominates B if every path from GC roots to B goes through A. Retained size of A = sum of shallow sizes of everything A dominates.

Workflow:

  1. Open dump (give MAT enough -Xmx in MemoryAnalyzer.ini, roughly 1-1.5x the dump for big ones; or run headless via ParseHeapDump.sh on a server).
  2. Leak Suspects report: flags objects (or accumulation points) retaining a large share; default threshold per the help is 10% of the heap.
  3. Dominator tree: sort by retained heap. Typical findings: one HashMap, an ArrayList in a singleton, a Thread (ThreadLocalMap), or a ClassLoader.
  4. Histogram: group by class to see counts. 40M char[]/byte[] or String points at text accumulation.
  5. Path to GC Roots, excluding weak/soft refs: shows the static or thread that pins it.
  6. Compare two dumps (taken 1 hour apart) with the histogram diff to see which class counts grow.
  7. OQL for targeted queries, e.g. SELECT * FROM java.util.HashMap WHERE size > 100000.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
(taking dumps)

jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /dumps/a.hprof          # preferred; live objects only by default
jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=/dumps/a.hprof <pid>   # "live" forces a full GC first

Note: jcmd GC.heap_dump dumps only live (reachable) objects by default (it runs a full GC first); -all includes unreachable ones. Verify for your JDK.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Looking at shallow size: a tiny object can retain gigabytes.
  • Keeping unreachable objects out of the dump and then wondering why a garbage-heavy pause is invisible: leaks only need reachable data, so that's fine, but allocation analysis needs JFR, not a dump.
  • Dumping a 28 GB heap on a loaded pod: the dump pauses the JVM for tens of seconds; do it on a drained instance.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can't I just sort by shallow heap? -> byte[]/char[] dominate but tell you nothing about the owner; the owner is found via retained size and GC-root paths.
  2. How to find who allocates, not who holds? -> A dump has no allocation sites; use JFR allocation events or async-profiler alloc.
  3. Dump too big to open? -> Headless MAT on a big box, or use jcmd to take a class histogram (GC.class_histogram) first to narrow.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "I open it in MAT and look at leak suspects". Senior explains retained vs shallow, drives from dominator tree to GC-root path, diffs two dumps, and handles dump cost/safety.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: The leak suspect was a 1.9 GB ConcurrentHashMap in a singleton with 60% of the heap; the GC-root path showed a static field in a metrics helper.

questions.promptHtml: How can a ThreadLocal cause a memory leak, especially on a servlet container or thread pool? How do you prevent it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Classic leak that combines GC reachability, thread pools, and classloaders, and a favorite in senior screens.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each Thread owns a ThreadLocalMap whose entries are weakly keyed by the ThreadLocal but strongly hold the value. Pool threads live as long as the pool, so a value you set on a request and never remove() stays reachable from the thread, which is a GC root. If the value, or its class, references a webapp classloader, it also blocks classloader unloading on redeploy. The fix: always remove() in a finally, and keep values small and few.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Thread (root, pooled, lives for days)
  -> threadLocals: ThreadLocalMap
       -> Entry[ WeakRef(ThreadLocal key) , strong value ]

When the ThreadLocal object itself becomes unreachable, the key goes null, and the stale entry is cleaned lazily on later get/set/remove calls on that map; there is no guarantee that this happens soon. If the thread never touches that map again, the value stays pinned. Plus: a value whose class was loaded by the webapp's classloader keeps the entire classloader (and all its classes, statics) alive: Metaspace growth after each redeploy.

Pool sizing makes it worse: 400 Tomcat threads x 5 MB cached buffer in a ThreadLocal = 2 GB that is never garbage and never "freed" under load.

Virtual threads also support ThreadLocal; but millions of them with per-thread caches multiply the cost, and scoped values are the intended alternative in newer releases (status per release: verify).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
private static final ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat> FMT =
        ThreadLocal.withInitial(() -> new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd"));

// BROKEN for request context: set but never cleared on a pooled thread
static void handle(Request r) {
    CTX.set(new RequestContext(r));
    process(r);              // exception or not, CTX stays
}

// FIXED
static void handleSafe(Request r) {
    CTX.set(new RequestContext(r));
    try { process(r); } finally { CTX.remove(); }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• set(null) instead of remove(): the entry stays.
  • Relying on the "weak key" to avoid leaks: the value is strong.
  • Putting a heavy per-thread cache (buffers, parsers) in a ThreadLocal with 500+ pool threads.
  • Stale data leaking between requests (a correctness/security bug) because a prior request's context wasn't cleared.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is the key weak? -> To let a ThreadLocal be collected when the owner dies; but values are strong, so it only partially helps.
  2. How to find it in a dump? -> MAT: filter for java.lang.ThreadLocal$ThreadLocalMap$Entry, look at retained size per Thread; path to GC roots from the value shows Thread.threadLocals.
  3. Alternative on modern JDK? -> ScopedValue (preview/final status depends on release: verify) or explicit context passing.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "ThreadLocals can leak, call remove". Senior explains weak-key/strong-value, why pools make it permanent, the classloader link, and finds it in MAT.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After each hot redeploy, Metaspace stepped up ~80 MB because one ThreadLocal in a library pinned the old classloader.

questions.promptHtml: What is a classloader leak? Why does it show up as OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace, and how do you diagnose and cap it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests understanding of class unloading rules and Metaspace sizing, relevant for app servers, plugin systems and runtime code generation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A class can be unloaded only when its ClassLoader is unreachable, which requires that all its classes, their instances and the loader itself are unreachable. If anything long-lived (a static in a parent loader, a pooled thread's ThreadLocal, a JDBC driver registration, a shutdown hook) references any of them, the whole loader stays and its metadata stays in Metaspace. Repeated redeploys or runtime class generation then grow Metaspace until it hits the cap or the container limit.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Since Java 8 (PermGen removed), class metadata lives in Metaspace, which is native memory. It is unbounded by default (MaxMetaspaceSize default is unlimited), so a leak grows RSS until the OS or container kills the process, not necessarily an OOM message. Setting -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize gives a clean, early OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace instead. -XX:MetaspaceSize is the threshold at which the first Metaspace-triggered GC occurs, not a cap.

Typical leak shapes:

  • Webapp redeploy: old loader pinned by a ThreadLocal, a java.sql.DriverManager registered driver, a logging framework holding appenders, or a timer thread started by the app.
  • Runtime generation: CGLIB/Byte Buddy/Javassist proxies or Groovy/script evaluation creating a new class per call; Proxy.newProxyInstance with a fresh loader each time; reflection inflation classes.
  • Lambdas/dynamic hidden classes are normally fine but a loop generating unique ones isn't.

Diagnosis:

jcmd <pid> VM.metaspace                 # per-loader breakdown (JDK 16+ detailed; verify earlier)
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram | head
jstat -gc <pid> 1000                    # MC/MU columns over time
-Xlog:class+unload=info -Xlog:gc+metaspace=info

In a heap dump, MAT's "Duplicate Classes" and the classloader explorer show many instances of the same loader; path-to-GC-roots from the old loader names the pinning reference.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// BROKEN: unique class generated per call, retained by a cache of Class objects
Class<?> c = new ByteBuddy().subclass(Object.class)
        .name("gen.Dyn" + System.nanoTime())
        .make().load(getClass().getClassLoader()).getLoaded();
// FIX: generate once per shape and cache; use a bounded set of names

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Setting MetaspaceSize thinking it caps memory.
  • Assuming Metaspace GC will clean up: it can't unload reachable loaders.
  • Setting MaxMetaspaceSize too low (e.g. 128 MB) for apps with thousands of classes (Spring + Hibernate commonly need 150-400 MB; measure).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does Metaspace count toward -Xmx? -> No, it's native memory outside the heap.
  2. Why does it matter in containers? -> RSS includes Metaspace; unbounded growth leads to an OOM kill.
  3. How can G1/ZGC unload classes? -> Class unloading happens at the end of concurrent marking (G1) or concurrently (ZGC); a leak means the loader stays marked.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "increase MaxMetaspaceSize". Senior: finds the reference that pins the loader, knows the default is unlimited, and uses the class-unload log plus a dump.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Hot-redeploy of a servlet app grew Metaspace ~80 MB per deploy until the instance needed a restart every 5 deploys.

questions.contextHtml:
An order service (Java 17, G1, -Xmx2g, 8 pods, ~300 RPS per pod) restarts every ~20 hours with java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space. Post-GC heap floor rises about 70 MB/hour. A recent feature added this in-memory idempotency guard to avoid duplicate processing:

@Service
class IdempotencyGuard {
    private final Map<String, OrderResult> seen = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    OrderResult process(String requestId, Supplier<OrderResult> work) {
        return seen.computeIfAbsent(requestId, id -> work.get());
    }
}

GC pauses are normal (G1 young ~25 ms), CPU is 40%, and the DBA says the database is healthy. The team suspects the new JSON library.
questions.promptHtml: Find the problem, explain how you'd prove it, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase heap to 4g" or "switch to ZGC". It treats the symptom, ignores the rising floor, and blames the JSON library without evidence.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did the leak start with the idempotency deploy (compare floor trend before/after)? Are request IDs unique per request or per client retry? Are 8 pods behind a random load balancer (so a per-pod map doesn't even deduplicate)? Is there a heap dump or a way to take one?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll pods on a schedule (rolling restart every 12 hours) and set -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError to a mounted volume; ExitOnOutOfMemoryError so pods recycle cleanly.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) the new seen map: unbounded, one entry per request. At 300 RPS x 3600 = 1.08M entries/hour; at ~65 bytes of key plus a result object of ~… that's consistent with ~70 MB/hour if the result is small. (2) The JSON library caching per-type data (bounded, unlikely to grow linearly). (3) Metrics cardinality. (4) A ThreadLocal.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare the floor trend graph in Prometheus (jvm_memory_used_bytes after GC, or jvm_gc_live_data_size_bytes) before and after the deploy. Take a dump with jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump, open in MAT, dominator tree: expect one ConcurrentHashMap with ~all retained size. Run GC.class_histogram twice, 30 minutes apart, to see OrderResult and String counts rising in step.
  5. Root cause: seen is a static-lifetime map (singleton bean) with no eviction, so every requestId stays reachable forever. The guard is also wrong in a second way: computeIfAbsent runs work.get() inside the map's bin lock, so a slow, blocking or recursive mapping function stalls other keys in the same bin and can throw on recursive updates. And per-pod memory does not deduplicate across 8 pods.
  6. Fix: Short term: a bounded, expiring cache (Caffeine maximumSize(100_000) and expireAfterWrite(10m)). Long term: idempotency belongs in a shared store (Redis SET NX EX, or a unique-constraint table) and work.get() should run outside of the map lock.
private final Cache<String, OrderResult> seen = Caffeine.newBuilder()
        .maximumSize(100_000).expireAfterWrite(Duration.ofMinutes(10)).build();
  1. Prevention: Review checklist: "every static/singleton collection has a bound and an eviction policy". A load test that runs 2 hours and asserts the post-GC floor slope is flat. Alert on jvm_gc_live_data_size_bytes slope.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't just grow the heap (delays the crash and lengthens full-GC pauses). A local cache doesn't give true idempotency across pods; accept it only as a best-effort optimization.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the TTL is 10 minutes, but memory still grows? -> Check the maximumSize is hit before TTL; entries' retained size may be larger than estimated; use Caffeine weigher.
  • Why not WeakHashMap? -> String keys created per request are weakly reachable almost immediately, so entries vanish at the next GC: it would deduplicate nothing.
  • Why does computeIfAbsent with a slow supplier hurt? -> It holds a bin lock; other threads with keys in that bin block, which can look like random latency.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "temporary" dedupe map survived two years because nothing alarmed on heap-floor slope; pods were restarted by a nightly cron nobody remembered, which hid the leak until the cron was removed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases heap or blames the library without evidence.
  • Hire: identifies unbounded map, proposes a bounded cache, and verifies with a heap dump.
  • Strong hire: also catches computeIfAbsent lock hold, per-pod semantics, uses the post-GC floor metric, and moves idempotency to a shared store.

questions.promptHtml: What does java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: GC overhead limit exceeded mean, and why is it often a better signal than plain heap OOM?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks understanding of GC thrashing and that this error is a heuristic, not a separate memory region.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: It is thrown when the JVM spends nearly all its time in GC while recovering almost nothing. For the Parallel collector the documented heuristic is more than 98% of time in GC and less than 2% of heap recovered, repeated over several consecutive collections. It means the live set is at or near the heap limit: the application is already effectively dead, crawling between full GCs. It is the same root problem as heap OOM (leak or undersized heap), just caught earlier.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Controlled by -XX:+UseGCOverheadLimit (on by default) with the Parallel collector; the 98%/2% thresholds come from the HotSpot docs and tuning guides (older, Parallel-centric; G1 behaves differently, and G1 usually goes to repeated Full GCs and then plain "Java heap space"; verify per version). Symptoms before the error: GC log shows back-to-back Full GCs, each freeing under 2%, GC time near 100%, CPU pinned on GC threads, request latency in seconds.

[Full GC (Ergonomics) 1990M->1985M(2000M), 3.8 s]
[Full GC (Ergonomics) 1991M->1988M(2000M), 3.9 s]
[Full GC (Ergonomics) 1992M->1990M(2000M), 4.0 s]   <- recovering <1%

Disabling the check (-XX:-UseGCOverheadLimit) just delays the failure and keeps the service in an unusable zombie state, so it is a bad idea except to get a diagnostic window.

Decision tree: Is the post-GC floor rising over hours (leak)? Or did it jump with a deploy/traffic change (undersized heap, oversized query result, batch job loading everything)? Or a one-off giant request (unbounded findAll())?

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Typical trigger: unbounded result set
List<Order> all = repo.findAll();         // 12M rows -> live set > heap
// Better: page / stream
try (Stream<Order> s = repo.streamAll()) { s.forEach(this::handle); }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Turning off the limit to "fix" it.
  • Increasing heap without checking if the data is needed.
  • Treating it as a CPU problem because CPU is 100%: that CPU is GC.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can it be thrown when heap is mostly free right before? -> It's a rate heuristic over consecutive collections; a sudden spike in live data can still trigger it.
  2. What would you page on? -> GC time ratio (jvm_gc_pause_seconds sum rate) and post-GC heap occupancy near 90%+.
  3. Does ZGC/Shenandoah throw it? -> Not in the same way; they can throw heap OOM or allocation stalls first. Verify per collector.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "heap is full". Senior: explains thrash heuristics, recognizes the log pattern, and checks leak versus workload change.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A reporting endpoint loading a month of orders took out a pod whose heap looked fine one minute earlier.

questions.promptHtml: How do you take a heap dump from a running production JVM safely, and what are the risks?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Practical competence: a dump can itself take down production.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Use jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump <path> (or jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=...). It is a stop-the-world operation proportional to the heap size: a 16 GB heap can freeze the process for tens of seconds and needs equal disk. So drain the instance from the load balancer first, write to a volume with enough space, and make sure -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError is already set for the crash case.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• jcmd GC.heap_dump by default dumps only reachable objects (it triggers a full GC first); -all (JDK 9+) includes unreachable ones. Verify the exact behavior for your JDK.
  • The dump runs inside the VM at a safepoint; health checks fail during it, so Kubernetes may kill the pod mid-dump (the liveness probe times out). Take the pod out of rotation and relax the probe, or use a debug copy.
  • Size: hprof is roughly the used heap size. 3 GB used => ~3 GB file. Compress before transfer.
  • kubectl cp of a multi-GB file is slow; prefer kubectl exec + upload to object storage.
  • Dumps contain PII, secrets and tokens: treat as sensitive data.
  • Alternatives when a full dump is too heavy: jcmd GC.class_histogram (cheap histogram, does a GC), JFR old-object sample (OldObjectSample event, low overhead, with path-to-root optional) to find leak candidates without a dump.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
jcmd 1 GC.heap_dump /dumps/svc-$(date +%s).hprof
jcmd 1 GC.class_histogram | head -30
jcmd 1 JFR.start name=leak settings=profile path-to-gc-roots=true duration=10m filename=/dumps/leak.jfr

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Running it on the only healthy pod during an incident.
  • Writing into /tmp in a read-only or small ephemeral FS.
  • Taking one dump: you can't see growth; take two spaced apart.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Container has 4 GB limit and heap is 3 GB; any risk? -> The dump writes through the page cache; mostly fine, but the pause and disk space are the real risks; page-cache pressure can count toward cgroup memory in some setups (verify).
  2. How does -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError work in a container kill? -> It doesn't; the kernel's SIGKILL gives no chance.
  3. Dump of a non-leaking heap? -> Live set composition for sizing and for finding duplicate strings/byte arrays.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "jmap -dump". Senior: knows the stop-the-world cost, probe-kill risk, disk and PII handling, and uses JFR/histograms as lighter alternatives.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A well-meaning on-call dumped a 24 GB heap on a live pod; the liveness probe killed it at 28 s and the dump was truncated and useless.

questions.promptHtml: What is a humongous object in G1, why does it cause trouble, and how do you detect and fix it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: G1 is the default since Java 9; humongous allocations are the most common self-inflicted G1 problem.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: In G1, any object at least half a region size is humongous. It's allocated directly into contiguous old-gen regions, bypassing young generation, and is never copied during evacuation. If there are many of them they fill old gen fast, trigger concurrent cycles early, fragment the heap and, in the worst case, cause Full GCs even with plenty of total free space. I detect it via GC logs and fix it by eliminating the large allocations, or by raising -XX:G1HeapRegionSize.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Region size is a power of two from 1 MB to 32 MB, chosen by ergonomics from heap size (target about 2048 regions). With a 4 GB heap the region is 2 MB, so the threshold is 1 MB. A 1.1 MB byte[] occupies one whole 2 MB region (0.9 MB wasted); a 2.1 MB array takes 2 regions (4 MB), wasting about 1.9 MB.

Region = 2 MB   humongous threshold = 1 MB
byte[1.1MB]  -> 1 region, ~45% wasted tail
byte[2.1MB]  -> 2 contiguous regions, ~48% wasted

Costs:

  • Allocation needs contiguous free regions; fragmentation can fail it even if total free is large.
  • Young collections do not reclaim them as part of normal young copying work, though recent JDKs can eagerly reclaim some dead humongous objects at young GC and the cleanup phase (G1EagerReclaimHumongousObjects, verify per version).
  • Humongous allocations count toward the IHOP trigger, so lots of them cause early/back-to-back concurrent cycles.
  • Large byte[] from a library (Kafka batches, JSON buffers, ByteArrayOutputStream growth, big ArrayList backing arrays, Jackson buffers) are the usual source.

Detection:

-Xlog:gc*,gc+humongous=debug:file=gc.log
# Log lines: "Pause Young (G1 Humongous Allocation)" or "GC Cause: G1 Humongous Allocation"
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info

JFR: jdk.ObjectAllocationOutsideTLAB shows the large allocation stack traces.

Fixes, in order: (1) stop allocating huge arrays: stream, chunk, reuse a pooled buffer; (2) cap ByteArrayOutputStream growth; (3) raise region size, e.g. -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=16m so that 4-7 MB arrays are no longer humongous (note: bigger regions mean fewer regions and coarser young sizing); (4) increase heap to ease fragmentation; (5) consider another collector.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// BROKEN: grows backing array, repeatedly creating huge arrays
ByteArrayOutputStream out = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
for (Chunk c : chunks) out.write(c.bytes());   // doubling copies up to 64 MB

// BETTER: stream to the sink
try (OutputStream os = sink.open()) { for (Chunk c : chunks) os.write(c.bytes()); }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Setting region size to 32 MB blindly: with a 2 GB heap that leaves 64 regions and hurts G1's ability to meet pause goals.
  • Looking only at pause time: humongous cost shows as early concurrent cycles and Full GCs.
  • Believing the "half region" rule is about total size including header: the exact rule is object size >= half the region size.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. 8 MB request body buffers, 4 GB heap: what do you do? -> Region is 2 MB, so each buffer takes 4 regions; use streaming/pooled buffers, or a 16 MB region (heap 4 GB => 256 regions; check that is acceptable).
  2. Does ZGC have humongous problems? -> It has size classes (small/medium/large pages) and no copying of large pages, so the issue is less acute; verify per version.
  3. Why are they never copied? -> Copying multi-MB objects would cost more than leaving them; they are reclaimed in place.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "big objects go to old gen". Senior: states the exact threshold, fragmentation and IHOP interplay, finds callers with JFR, and picks between code change and region size.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Kafka consumer batching 3 MB payloads caused a Full GC every few minutes on a 6 GB heap; raising region size and capping batch size ended it.

questions.contextHtml: A Java 17 service runs in Kubernetes with resources.limits.memory: 2Gi and JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-Xmx1536m. About every 36 hours, pods restart with Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137. Heap graphs show used heap peaking at about 900 MB, no Java exception, no hs_err file. The container working-set metric climbs gradually over a day and a half to 2 GiB. The service uses Netty-based HTTP client, ~220 threads, and serves ~400 RPS. Last month someone raised Xmx from 1g to 1.5g "for headroom".
questions.promptHtml: What is happening and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Memory leak, take a heap dump". The heap is fine, and the process was SIGKILLed, so no dump or exception exists. Or "just raise the container limit".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the kill triggered by container working set (cgroup) rather than JVM OOM (check kubectl describe pod, dmesg)? Is RSS growth steady (leak) or sawtooth (arena fragmentation)? What libraries use native memory (Netty, compression, JNI)? Is NMT enabled? What changed a month ago besides Xmx?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Lower Xmx back to ~1g (or set -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=50) to restore native headroom, and add a rolling restart schedule shorter than 36 hours while investigating.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) Container budget was never sized for non-heap: Xmx 1.5g of 2g leaves 512 MB for Metaspace (~100-150 MB), code cache (up to 240 MB reserved with tiered), 220 thread stacks (220 x ~1 MB = ~220 MB reserved, committed as touched), GC structures, direct buffers. That fits. (2) Netty direct buffers leaking or pooled arenas growing. (3) glibc malloc arena fragmentation (many threads x 8 x cores arenas). (4) Thread count growth. Red herring: "heap leak", since heap peaks at 900 MB.
  4. How I'd verify each: Enable -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary (costs a small overhead; verify for the JDK). jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory baseline, wait hours under load, then jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary.diff. Compare against process RSS (/proc/<pid>/status VmRSS, or pmap -x). If NMT total grows with RSS => JVM-internal (threads, metaspace, code). If RSS grows more than NMT => glibc arenas or JNI/native libs. Check Netty PlatformDependent.usedDirectMemory() and the java.nio:type=BufferPool,name=direct MBean.
  5. Root cause: Suppose NMT shows heap committed 1.4 GB (because Xmx 1.5g let the heap expand and G1 doesn't give memory back quickly), thread ~250 MB, metaspace 130 MB, code ~60 MB, plus 100+ MB of direct buffers: total ~2 GB. The raise of Xmx plus a normal slow rise in committed heap pushed RSS over the 2 GiB cgroup limit. Used heap is 900 MB but committed heap is not used heap.
  6. Fix: Short term: Xmx ~ 1g, -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=256m to turn buffer leaks into catchable errors, -Xss512k if code allows, MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 if NMT shows gaps. Long term: size by budget: container limit = heap + metaspace + code + threads + direct + ~10-20% slack; prefer -XX:MaxRAMPercentage of 50-65% for small containers.
-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=60 -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=192m -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=256m
-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary
  1. Prevention: Dashboard RSS/working set next to heap used and committed; alert at 85% of the container limit; load test with the production container limits; memory budget table in the service README.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I won't just raise the limit to 4Gi (cost, hides the budget bug). I won't enable NMT detail in prod (higher overhead). I won't take heap dumps for this.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• NMT total is flat but RSS grows 5 MB/hour? -> Native allocator fragmentation or JNI/native lib; try MALLOC_ARENA_MAX, jemalloc, or pmap diffs.
  • Why does committed heap stay high? -> G1 returns memory to the OS only at certain points (periodic uncommit options exist in newer JDKs: verify G1PeriodicGCInterval), so committed ≈ max reached.
  • Does -XX:MaxRAMPercentage apply with explicit Xmx? -> No, explicit -Xmx wins.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team "fixed" OOMKills by raising the limit three times; each time the kill interval merely stretched. The real fix was a Netty buffer path that retained pooled buffers on an error branch.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: asks for a heap dump or only raises memory.
  • Hire: identifies non-heap budget, uses NMT, and re-sizes heap properly.
  • Strong hire: contrasts NMT with RSS to identify glibc/JNI gaps, bounds direct memory, adds alerting, and explains committed vs used heap.

questions.promptHtml: Explain Native Memory Tracking. How do you use it, and what does it not tell you?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Off-heap leaks are the hardest class; this separates seniors who know the limits of their tools.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: NMT is a HotSpot feature that tracks the JVM's own native allocations by category (heap, class, thread, code, GC, internal, symbols, etc.). Enable it with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary (or detail), take a baseline with jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory baseline, then summary.diff later to see which category grew. It does not see memory allocated by native libraries through their own malloc, JNI code, or glibc arena fragmentation, so I compare NMT's total against the process RSS to find the gap.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Flags and commands (documented for Java 8+ and similar later):

-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=off|summary|detail     (default off)
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory baseline
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary.diff
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory detail.diff          # call sites; heavier

Overhead: summary is modest and detail is heavier; one source cites a 5-10% slowdown (verify for your JDK; do not quote as a guarantee). Enabling NMT requires a restart, so turn it on proactively for services with large off-heap use.

Categories: Java Heap, Class (Metaspace), Thread (stacks), Code, GC (remembered sets, bitmaps, can be 10-20% of heap with G1 on big heaps), Compiler, Internal, Symbol, Native Memory Tracking itself, Arena Chunk, Shared class space.

Interpreting: committed (not reserved) approximates real use. The relationship:

RSS  ~=  NMT committed total  +  libs/JNI/mmap'd files  +  glibc fragmentation overhead

When RSS >> NMT: suspect glibc arenas (default up to 8 x CPU arenas per process on 64-bit; MALLOC_ARENA_MAX), native libraries (compression, SSL, RocksDB, image libraries), or mmap'd files. Use pmap -x <pid> snapshots, /proc/<pid>/smaps, jemalloc/tcmalloc profiling, or Linux perf/bpftrace for malloc call sites.

Direct ByteBuffers are tracked in NMT only under "Other"/Internal-ish categories depending on version (verify), so also check BufferPoolMXBean.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import java.lang.management.*;
for (BufferPoolMXBean b : ManagementFactory.getPlatformMXBeans(BufferPoolMXBean.class)) {
    System.out.printf("%s count=%d used=%d capacity=%d%n",
        b.getName(), b.getCount(), b.getMemoryUsed(), b.getTotalCapacity());
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reading reserved as consumption.
  • Believing NMT shows everything: it's JVM-internal only.
  • Enabling detail in prod without testing the cost.
  • Forgetting the thread category: 2000 threads x 1 MB is 2 GB reserved.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. RSS 3.1 GB, NMT total committed 2.2 GB. Where do you look? -> The 900 MB gap: glibc arenas, native libs, mmap'd files; pmap diff, MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2, try jemalloc.
  2. How is Metaspace shown? -> Under Class with metadata; also jcmd VM.metaspace for detail.
  3. How would you attribute a leak to code? -> detail.diff for JVM call sites; for native libs use malloc profilers.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE has never used it. Senior uses baseline/diff, knows reserved vs committed, and knows the NMT-vs-RSS gap as the clue for non-JVM allocators.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A gRPC/compression stack leaked 1.2 GB over 3 days through glibc arenas; NMT was flat, RSS was not.

questions.promptHtml: What causes OutOfMemoryError: Direct buffer memory, how is direct memory limited, and how do you debug it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Netty, gRPC, Kafka clients and NIO make this common, and heap graphs mislead.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: ByteBuffer.allocateDirect allocates native memory, limited by -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize (defaulting to roughly the max heap size). The memory is freed only when the small on-heap DirectByteBuffer object is garbage collected (via a Cleaner), so lots of direct allocation with little heap pressure means GC rarely runs and the limit is hit while the heap looks fine. Netty avoids this with pooled buffers and reference counting, and leaks appear when a ByteBuf isn't released.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
When allocating, the JDK's Bits.reserveMemory checks the budget; if exceeded, it calls System.gc() to try to free unreachable buffers, sleeps briefly, retries, then throws OOM. That is why explicit -XX:+DisableExplicitGC can make direct-memory OOMs worse (the fallback GC becomes a no-op). -XX:+ExplicitGCInvokesConcurrent is the alternative for G1.

Causes:

  • Netty ByteBuf not released (missing release(), exception paths) or too-big pooled arenas.
  • Many threads each creating cached temporary direct buffers (the JDK caches per-thread temp buffers for NIO channel IO; large heap-buffer writes to channels may allocate big direct temps: jdk.nio.maxCachedBufferSize limits it).
  • Allocation of large buffers per request without pooling.

Debug:

BufferPoolMXBean "direct" (count, used, capacity)       # Micrometer: jvm_buffer_memory_used_bytes{id="direct"}
-Dio.netty.leakDetection.level=paranoid                  # staging only; high cost
-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=512m                             # make failures explicit/early

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
ByteBuf buf = ctx.alloc().directBuffer(8192);
try {
    // use buf
} finally {
    buf.release();      // forgetting this leaks pooled memory
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Relying on -Xmx to bound off-heap memory.
  • Using -XX:+DisableExplicitGC with heavy direct buffer use.
  • Leak detection paranoid in production (use simple sampling).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is the default tied to Xmx? -> Historical choice: if unset, Runtime.maxMemory() is used; verify the exact rule for your JDK.
  2. Heap 1 GB, direct limit 1 GB, container 1.5 GB: problem? -> Worst-case RSS exceeds the container: need to budget direct memory explicitly.
  3. Memory-mapped files (MappedByteBuffer)? -> Not counted in MaxDirectMemorySize; shows in RSS and page cache.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "increase MaxDirectMemorySize". Senior: knows the Cleaner/GC dependency, explicit GC fallback, Netty refcounting, and budgets direct memory inside the container.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A proxy service hit direct OOM at 70% heap-free because young GC ran every 90 s while 8 KB buffers per connection accumulated.

questions.promptHtml: You see java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread. What are the possible causes, and how do you tell them apart?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It looks like a memory error but is usually OS or thread-leak related; heap tuning makes it worse.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The JVM asked the OS for a thread and was refused. Three families: too many threads (leak or unbounded pool, hitting ulimit -u or cgroup pids.max), not enough native memory for stacks (each thread reserves -Xss, default 1 MB on 64-bit Linux, and the container limit or address space is exhausted), or kernel limits (kernel.threads-max, vm.max_map_count). I count threads with a thread dump, then check limits.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Each Java platform thread maps to an OS thread with its own stack. 10,000 threads x 1 MB = ~10 GB of reserved virtual memory, committed as touched. Heap sized too large leaves less room for stacks in a container: raising Xmx can trigger this.

Diagnosis:

jcmd <pid> Thread.print | grep -c '^"'          # thread count
ls /proc/<pid>/task | wc -l
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/pids.max ; cat /sys/fs/cgroup/pids.current   # cgroup v2
ulimit -u                                        # per-user process/thread limit
cat /proc/sys/vm/max_map_count                   # each thread uses several mappings

Group thread names in the dump (pool-17-thread-N, http-nio-8080-exec, ForkJoinPool) to find who is multiplying. A newCachedThreadPool() under a burst, or a new Executor created per request and never shut down, are classic sources.

Fixes: bounded pools with queues and rejection policy, reuse executors, reduce -Xss (only if deep recursion isn't needed), raise limits where legitimate, or use virtual threads to remove the thread-per-request ceiling (see the virtual-threads chunk).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// BROKEN: new pool per request; never shut down
void handle() {
    ExecutorService ex = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(16);
    ex.submit(this::work);                 // 16 threads leaked per call
}
// FIXED: one shared, bounded, named pool
private static final ExecutorService POOL = new ThreadPoolExecutor(16, 16, 0, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
        new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1000), new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Increasing heap in response.
  • Raising ulimit without finding why the count grew.
  • Blaming the OS when the app leaked threads.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Container pids.max=1024, app has 600 threads; failures at random? -> Count all threads including JVM internal (GC, compiler, carrier); also fork by subprocess counts.
  2. How is a leaked thread different from a busy one? -> A leaked one is parked or idle in a pool nobody uses; dumps show the same stack across hundreds of threads.
  3. What changes with virtual threads? -> Virtual threads are heap objects and don't consume OS threads each, so this OOM moves to other limits (carrier threads, memory).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "too many threads". Senior checks cgroup pids.max, stack math, thread-dump grouping by name, and fixes the creation pattern.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A retry helper created an executor per failed call; during a downstream outage the service spawned 30k threads in minutes.

questions.subtopic: Long pauses not caused by GC work
questions.promptHtml: The GC log says a pause was 40 ms of GC work but the application saw a 1.8 s stall. What non-GC causes of "GC-looking" pauses do you know and how do you find them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors know the JVM is not the only source of stalls: safepoints, OS and container behavior.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I compare wall time to CPU time in the GC log (user, sys, real). If real is much bigger than user+sys/threads, the JVM was waiting on something: swapping, CPU throttling by the cgroup, a slow disk writing the GC log, or time-to-safepoint where threads take long to reach a safepoint. I then check safepoint logs (-Xlog:safepoint), cgroup throttling counters, swap, THP, and noisy neighbors.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Stop-the-world pause = time to reach safepoint (TTSP) + the operation itself. GC log "Pause" typically shows only the operation; threads in long counted loops without safepoint polls (less common since loop strip mining in newer JDKs) or in slow JNI can delay it. Unified logging:

-Xlog:safepoint*=info:file=safepoint.log:time,uptime
# "Safepoint "G1CollectForAllocation", Time since last: ..., Reaching safepoint: 1650 ms, At safepoint: 38 ms"

Other causes:

  • CPU throttling: a container with cpu limit: 2 has CFS quota; GC threads burst and get throttled; container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total rises. Pauses stretch even though GC work is small.
  • Swap or memory pressure: a heap partly swapped makes GC page in; real >> user+sys, high sys time.
  • Transparent Huge Pages compaction, NUMA effects: high sys time in GC lines.
  • GC log on slow/blocked disk: logging is synchronous by default unless -Xlog async is used (async logging exists in newer JDKs: verify version).
  • VM-level stalls: hypervisor steal time, live migration.
  • Allocation stalls / concurrent mode failures that appear as long pauses of a different type.

GC log line example:

[gc] GC(142) Pause Young (Normal) 1920M->410M(4096M) 38.211ms
[gc,cpu] GC(142) User=0.09s Sys=1.44s Real=0.04s   # big Sys => OS interference

(Interpret: Sys is high; investigate THP/swap.)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
(checks)

cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat           # nr_throttled, throttled_usec
vmstat 1 ; sar -B ; free -m           # swapping, paging
-Xlog:gc*,safepoint:file=/logs/gc.log:time,uptime

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Tuning G1 flags when GC work is only 40 ms.
  • Ignoring that application-level stalls (lock contention, DNS, downstream) can look like GC when you only correlate time.
  • Looking at p50 rather than max pause.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you know it's TTSP? -> Safepoint log's "Reaching safepoint" is large; find the thread via -XX:+SafepointTimeout -XX:SafepointTimeoutDelay=... (verify flags per version).
  2. CPU limit 1 and 4 GC threads? -> Throttling; set CPU requests and avoid tight CPU limits for latency services, or size ParallelGCThreads.
  3. How do you tell a GC pause from an app stall? -> JFR jdk.GCPhasePause vs thread state events; a common system-level monitor like jHiccup shows platform stalls independent of GC.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "GC pause, tune GC". Senior distinguishes TTSP, OS and cgroup effects using real vs user/sys, and the safepoint log.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 1.5 s p99 spike disappeared after removing a CPU limit that was throttling the pod 18% of periods.

questions.contextHtml:
A Java 17 G1 service (heap 8 GB, region 4 MB, so humongous threshold 2 MB) exposes a CSV export endpoint. After a feature release, p99 goes from 180 ms to 4.5 s every few minutes; throughput normal otherwise (RPS 600, CPU 55%). GC logs:

[gc] GC(311) Pause Young (G1 Humongous Allocation) 5120M->3980M(8192M) 212.4ms
[gc] GC(312) Pause Young (Concurrent Start) (G1 Humongous Allocation) 5400M->4900M(8192M) 301.9ms
[gc] GC(313) Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 7900M->3100M(8192M) 3920.1ms

Heap used after concurrent cycle floor ~3 GB. The new export builds the whole file in a ByteArrayOutputStream, with typical files 20-40 MB. Someone proposes "switch to ZGC".
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix this.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Increase heap or change collector with no cause analysis. Misses that the log's pause cause names humongous allocation.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many concurrent exports (each 40 MB buffer doubles, copying 64 MB arrays)? Did pauses begin with the feature release? Is the Full GC frequency correlated with export requests? JDK build (some humongous reclaim fixes differ)? Is memory limit tied to container?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Rate-limit or disable the export endpoint (feature flag); if needed, set -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=16m as a stop-gap (threshold 8 MB).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) Humongous allocations from ByteArrayOutputStream growth (arrays of 2 MB, 4, 8, ... 64 MB, each is humongous). (2) Concurrent cycle starting too late, causing evacuation failure then Full GC. (3) Old-gen live-set growth. (4) Remembered-set overhead (red herring until the log says so).
  4. How I'd verify each: GC log cause strings ("G1 Humongous Allocation"); -Xlog:gc+humongous=debug or gc+heap=debug; JFR jdk.ObjectAllocationOutsideTLAB to see stack traces allocating >2 MB; correlate with endpoint access logs; GC logs Humongous Regions: before->after in the heap summary.
  5. Root cause: Each export, by doubling the buffer, creates humongous arrays totaling roughly 2x file size (e.g. 32 MB + 16 + 8 ... ~64 MB of regions for a 40 MB file); with 20 concurrent exports that's ~1.3 GB of contiguous humongous regions. They go straight to old gen, push occupancy past IHOP (default 45%) and need contiguous regions; fragmentation plus an underestimated need caused to-space/evacuation failures and a 3.9 s Full GC.
  6. Fix: Short term: cap concurrency on export, region size 16m. Long term: stream rows directly to the HTTP response or object storage:
@GetMapping("/export")
StreamingResponseBody export() {
    return out -> {
        try (var w = new BufferedWriter(new OutputStreamWriter(out, UTF_8), 64 * 1024)) {
            repo.streamRows().forEach(r -> write(w, r));   // constant memory
        }
    };
}
  1. Prevention: Code review flag: ByteArrayOutputStream, readAllBytes, toByteArray on unbounded input. Alert on jvm_gc_pause_seconds{cause="G1 Humongous Allocation"} and on Full GC count. A load test with realistic export sizes.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't switch collectors first: ZGC may hide the symptom but the 64 MB per request copy still burns memory bandwidth and RSS. A big region size reduces region count, which affects pause prediction. I'd avoid raising IHOP hacks before removing the allocation.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Export must be a single sorted file in memory? -> Write to a temp file or object storage with multipart upload, return a download link.
  • Heap 2 GB instead of 8 GB? -> Region 1 MB, threshold 512 KB: even moderate buffers become humongous; streaming matters more.
  • Why not just -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=32m? -> Fewer, coarser regions limit young-gen sizing granularity and may harm pause goals on small heaps.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "temporary" batch export lived for years with a 10-minute Full GC every morning; the actual fix was a 12-line change to stream to disk.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes heap or switches GC without cause.
  • Hire: identifies humongous allocation from the log and streams.
  • Strong hire: quantifies buffer doubling, IHOP and fragmentation, uses JFR for allocation stacks, adds alerts/code-review rules.

questions.contextHtml:
A Java 21 service (G1, Xmx 12 GB, 4 CPU, 10k RPS aggregate over 20 pods) is stable for months. After a Monday deploy that added a 3 GB in-memory reference-data cache per pod (loaded at startup), the p99 jumps from 90 ms to 1.2 s during peak. GC logs at peak:

[gc] GC(88) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 9800M->8900M(12288M) 640.3ms
[gc] To-space exhausted
[gc] GC(91) Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 11800M->5400M(12288M) 5210.5ms

Allocation rate ~900 MB/s. The old gen after mixed cycles sits around 5.4 GB. -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100 is set. The team's idea: "halve the pause target to 50 ms".
questions.promptHtml: What is going on and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Lowers MaxGCPauseMillis, which makes G1 shrink young and collect more often, worsening it. Doesn't recognize "To-space exhausted".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did old-gen occupancy before the cache deploy sit lower (maybe 2.4 GB)? Are there concurrent marking cycles in the log, and did they finish before the heap filled? Any custom G1 flags (IHOP, reserve)? Is the cache a few huge arrays/maps (humongous)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back the cache or reduce its size; or increase heap to 16 GB (if the node permits) to restore headroom.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) Live set rose by 3 GB, so old gen at 5.4 GB is 45% of 12 GB: concurrent marking now starts continuously and has less headroom; at 900 MB/s allocation, G1 runs out of free regions before mixed collections reclaim enough. (2) "To-space exhausted" = evacuation failure: survivors/promotions had no free regions to copy into. (3) Humongous cache structures. (4) Too-low pause target causing tiny young gen and premature promotion.
  4. How I'd verify each: GC logs: concurrent cycle start/end times vs. heap fill (-Xlog:gc*,gc+ergo*=debug); check "Concurrent Mark Cycle" duration; look at G1 reserve percent and IHOP adaptive value. jstat -gcutil for old %, JFR GC timeline.
  5. Root cause: Not enough free headroom for the allocation rate: the adaptive IHOP target is tied to old-gen size and the pause target, but with a 3 GB larger permanent live set, marking began too late or couldn't complete before survivors needed space. When G1 can't find a free region to copy survivors, it hits an evacuation failure ("to-space exhausted") and falls back to a Full GC (single-threaded in older JDKs; parallel full GC arrived in JDK 10).
  6. Fix: Short term: increase heap to ~16 GB so the 5.4 GB live set is ~34%, and restore the pause target to 200 ms (the default) to let G1 size young properly. Consider -XX:G1ReservePercent modestly higher (default 10; verify) as a safety margin. Long term: move the 3 GB cache off-heap or out of process (Caffeine with size limits, or an external store), or consider generational ZGC for large live sets with strict latency (Java 21: -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational; verify since the default changed in later releases).
-Xms16g -Xmx16g -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200 -Xlog:gc*,gc+ergo*=debug:file=gc.log
  1. Prevention: Capacity-test heap headroom with each cache addition. Alert on To-space exhausted and any Full GC. Track live-set (post-GC) as a first-class metric with budget per service.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't set IHOP very low blindly (more concurrent cycles burn CPU). A larger heap costs money per pod: 20 pods x 4 GB = 80 GB. Generational ZGC trades throughput/CPU and memory overhead for pause stability.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Same load, heap fixed to 16 GB, still seeing mixed GC long pauses? -> Check remembered set sizes and mixed-collection candidate selection (G1MixedGCCountTarget, G1HeapWastePercent), and old-region liveness thresholds.
  • Why is Full GC 5 s on 12 GB? -> Compacts the whole heap using parallel threads; time scales with live data and thread count (4 CPUs only).
  • Would -Xms=-Xmx matter? -> Avoids resize pauses and commit churn; in containers it reserves more RSS up front.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "small" lookup cache doubled live set; the GC dashboard showed no flags changed, but the live-set metric had jumped the same day, and nobody was watching it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: halves the pause target or only adds heap blindly.
  • Hire: identifies evacuation failure from the log and live-set growth and adds heap/headroom.
  • Strong hire: ties IHOP, reserve, allocation rate and mark duration together, proposes cache off-heap or ZGC with trade-offs, and adds alerts.

questions.contextHtml: A Java 17 payments gateway (G1, Xmx 4 GB, 16 pods) has no OOMs but every pod needs a restart after ~9 days because p99 degrades from 120 ms to 900 ms. At day 8, young GCs take 90 ms (from 20 ms), mixed GCs are frequent, and the post-GC floor is 3.1 GB (from 1.2 GB on day 1). A heap dump from a day-8 pod (3.4 GB) shows: 1.6 GB retained by io.micrometer.core.instrument.composite.CompositeMeterRegistry via ~2.4M Meter objects, tag values like uri=/users/8f4c-... and userId=.... CPU is moderate; threads stable at 140. Team lead says "it's Metaspace-like, maybe a classloader thing".
questions.promptHtml: Explain the cause and a full fix, including what to do about the existing metrics.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames the GC (switch to ZGC) or says "restart nightly". Doesn't connect meter count to label cardinality.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Where do userId and the full URI become tags (HTTP server metrics default uri uses the route template, so a raw path means a custom filter or a client metric)? Is the Prometheus scrape time also rising? Does the monitoring backend bill by series?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Deploy a MeterFilter that denies or maps high-cardinality tags, and rolling-restart pods; reduce scrape load meanwhile.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) Unbounded tag cardinality creating a meter per unique value. (2) Retained per-request objects in a tracing/MDC layer. (3) Metaspace (red herring: the dump and floor point at heap objects). (4) A large cache.
  4. How I'd verify each: MAT dominator tree: top retainer, then group by class and look at Meter$Id tag values; count series: /actuator/prometheus | wc -l, or meterRegistry.getMeters().size() via an endpoint; two dumps diffed to confirm linear growth ~ requests.
  5. Root cause: Micrometer keeps a Meter per unique (name, tag set) forever in the registry (static lifetime); a tag fed by user id or raw URL grows without bound. Each meter plus its timer histogram buckets costs hundreds of bytes to KBs: 2.4M x ~650 bytes = ~1.56 GB, matching the dump. Larger live set means longer young and mixed GC, which is why latency degraded gradually.
  6. Fix: Short term: filter.
registry.config().meterFilter(MeterFilter.deny(id ->
        id.getTags().stream().anyMatch(t -> t.getKey().equals("userId"))));
registry.config().meterFilter(MeterFilter.maximumAllowableTags(
        "http.server.requests", "uri", 100, MeterFilter.deny()));

Long term: use route templates for uri, put identifiers in logs and traces, not metrics; use exemplars where needed. 7. Prevention: Metric review checklist (every tag has a bounded value set); an alert on jvm_gc_live_data_size_bytes slope and on series count per metric; a test that hits the endpoint with 10k random IDs and asserts meter count stays flat. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I won't just raise the heap to 8 GB (cost, and Prometheus will also suffer from the series). I'd avoid removing the metric entirely; keep bounded dimensions so dashboards still work.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Metrics backend suddenly bills 10x? -> Same root cause; series count equals cost.
  • Can we remove old meters? -> registry.remove(meter) or meter filters with expiry (MeterFilter + Micrometer's meter TTL in some registries); better to not create them.
  • Why did the heap dump look "normal" for a Java developer? -> The retained objects are inside a library; only the dominator path reveals it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A new "customer tier" tag was added by a well-meaning dev; with customer ids as values, the metrics endpoint grew to 40 MB per scrape and the scraper timed out before the heap ever did.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restarts or changes collector.
  • Hire: finds Micrometer cardinality via MAT and filters tags.
  • Strong hire: quantifies per-meter cost, links to GC degradation, and adds guardrails (filter, tests, alerts).

questions.contextHtml: A fleet of 60 pods runs a Java 17 G1 service with -Xmx6g and container limit 8Gi (cost: 60 x 8 GiB). Dashboards show post-GC heap floor of 1.4 GB, peak used heap 2.8 GB, young GC every 4 s at ~30 ms, no Full GCs, p99 = 140 ms, SLO 300 ms. Finance asks you to halve memory cost. A colleague proposes "set -Xmx2g and limit 3Gi".
questions.promptHtml: How do you decide new sizes and roll it out safely?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Cuts to the proposed numbers without computing headroom, or refuses because "GC needs memory".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What are the worst-case traffic and batch events (daily peak, failover to fewer pods)? Is the live set stable over the week (no leak)? How much non-heap memory does RSS show (NMT, Netty)? What's the allocation rate?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (no incident); change under canary.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) The live set of 1.4 GB (floor) is small, so heap 3-4 GB is enough. (2) A 2 GB heap leaves only 0.6 GB above the 1.4 GB floor (~30% headroom), too tight for G1 with 1+ GB/s allocation. (3) Non-heap may need 600-900 MB, so 3 GiB container is too small. (4) A pod-count trade-off: fewer, bigger pods vs. more small pods.
  4. How I'd verify each: Weekly p99 of post-GC floor; allocation rate from jstat/GC log; RSS vs heap committed; NMT snapshot; load test at 1.5x peak with candidate settings and compare p99, GC frequency, pause time and CPU.
  5. Root cause: N/A. The decision rule: heap ~ 2.5-3x live set to keep GC cheap (a rule of thumb; measure), so 1.4 GB floor suggests ~4 GB. Container = heap + non-heap (say 0.8 GB) + 15% slack: about 5.5 Gi.
  6. Fix: Roll out -Xmx4g, container 5.5Gi (saves ~31% memory), using -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 equivalent only if consistent. Canary 3 pods for a week including a peak, comparing: GC time ratio (<5%), young pause p99, Full GC = 0, RSS < 85% of limit. If good, step to 3.5g. Consider fewer larger pods: the per-pod overhead (non-heap, ~800 MB) is paid 60 times; 30 pods with 8 GB total would save more.
-Xms4g -Xmx4g
  1. Prevention: Right-sizing dashboards (live set, RSS, GC ratio), quarterly review, alert at RSS 85% and at GC time over 8%.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't size on peak used heap (garbage inflates it). I wouldn't go to 2g: higher GC frequency, CPU cost, and the risk of OOM during traffic spikes outweigh savings. Smaller pods also reduce JIT sharing and may increase p99 via warmup overhead at autoscale.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Move to ZGC to run tighter? -> ZGC needs headroom too (concurrent collection requires free space) and has memory overhead; not for cost cutting alone.
  • What if CPU becomes the constraint after shrinking? -> GC threads compete; watch CPU% and throttling.
  • Metaspace/direct usage doubled in the canary? -> Re-budget; those don't shrink with heap.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team halved memory and saved 40% cost, then the quarterly batch spike took out the pods; the canary week had not included month-end.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: random numbers or a flat refusal.
  • Hire: uses live set to size heap and adds container overhead.
  • Strong hire: canary with explicit success metrics, covers non-heap, pod count trade-off, and rare peaks.

questions.contextHtml: A trading-adjacent API (Java 21, G1, Xmx 24 GB, 8 CPUs, 3,000 RPS/pod, SLO p99.9 < 50 ms) shows G1 pauses of 80-300 ms every few minutes (live set 11 GB). The team wants to migrate to generational ZGC (-XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational in Java 21; verify the flag for your release). Constraint: no downtime, and the same service must keep its CPU budget (already 65% on average).
questions.promptHtml: Should we migrate? How do you plan and execute it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "ZGC has sub-millisecond pauses, so just flip the flag everywhere." Ignores CPU overhead, memory overhead, throughput, and allocation stalls.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are the SLO breaches caused by GC (correlate pauses with p99.9)? What is allocation rate (ZGC needs headroom to finish concurrent cycles before allocation outruns it)? Is the process CPU-bound? JDK 21 vs 25 (generational is default in later releases: verify)? Any JNI or flags specific to G1?
  2. Immediate mitigation: If breaches hurt now: lower MaxGCPauseMillis only after confirming cause; add heap headroom (live set 11 GB of 24 is 46%).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) Pauses are real GC (mixed collections/evacuation) so ZGC helps. (2) Some tail latency comes from non-GC (safepoints, throttling), which ZGC won't fix. (3) CPU headroom is insufficient for concurrent GC threads. (4) Allocation stalls under spikes.
  4. How I'd verify each: Overlay GC pause timeline with p99.9 latency; JFR; -Xlog:safepoint. Then a staging replay (production traffic capture) with ZGC, comparing p99.9, CPU, RSS and throughput. Watch ZGC logs for "Allocation Stall".
  5. Root cause: G1 pause time depends on live data copied and remembered-set work per collection; at 11 GB live with high mutation, mixed pauses exceed the SLO. ZGC does marking and relocation concurrently using load barriers and colored pointers, so pause times stay roughly independent of heap size (typically sub-millisecond to low milliseconds; verify with measurements), at the cost of barrier overhead, concurrent CPU use and memory (multi-mapping inflates virtual not physical).
  6. Fix (plan): Stage 1: replay-test on 1 canary, ZGC heap bumped to 28-30 GB since ZGC wants headroom. Stage 2: 5% of pods with ZGC behind the same load balancer, compare against G1 pods on identical traffic (A/B by pod). Stage 3: ramp 25% / 50% / 100% over a week; keep the G1 flag set ready for rollback (a config flip and rolling restart).
-XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational   (Java 21)
-Xms28g -Xmx28g -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log
  1. Prevention: SLO dashboards per collector; alert on allocation stalls, GC CPU share, and RSS; load test in CI for GC-sensitive changes.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Non-generational ZGC in Java 21 needs more headroom for high allocation rates; generational ZGC is meant for that. I wouldn't migrate without a CPU plan: average 65% CPU plus concurrent GC may need extra pods. I wouldn't switch on the whole fleet at once, and wouldn't keep G1 tuning flags (MaxGCPauseMillis, IHOP) that ZGC ignores.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Canary shows p99.9 fine but CPU +12%? -> Pay for it with more pods or more headroom; compare cost vs SLO penalty.
  • Allocation stalls appear at spikes? -> Increase heap or reduce allocation; ZGC stalls threads when it cannot reclaim fast enough.
  • Why not Shenandoah? -> Comparable concurrent design; availability and support depend on the JDK vendor build; evaluate with the same replay.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A migration looked flawless on average latency; only the p99.9 panel showed that the 3 s "cold" stalls were JIT deopt storms, not GC at all. The team caught it because the A/B was run per pod.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: flips the flag everywhere or dismisses it.
  • Hire: tests in staging and canary, notes memory/CPU overhead.
  • Strong hire: validates GC is the cause first, A/B by pod, sizes headroom, defines rollback and success metrics, knows version-specific flags and defaults.
